removed.title: Interaction-type legend strip
removed.text:
Print one per pair as a narrow strip (can be cut from the bottom of the profile card sheet).

COLOUR CODE FOR ARROWS:
• Colour 1 — Biotic–biotic interaction
• Colour 2 — Biotic–abiotic interaction
• Colour 3 — Abiotic–abiotic interaction

FIVE RELATIONSHIP TYPES TO LABEL:
• Predation / herbivory (one organism eats another)
• Mutualism (both organisms benefit)
• Commensalism (one benefits, one unaffected)
• Parasitism (one benefits, one harmed)
• Competition (both organisms compete for the same resource)
• Decomposer role (breaks down dead matter, releases nutrients to abiotic environment)

TROPHIC LEVEL REMINDER:
A trophic level is a feeding position in a food chain. Producers are Level 1; primary consumers (eat producers) are Level 2; secondary consumers (eat primary consumers) are Level 3; and so on.

periods.activity_description: Students explore two contrasting habitats — a pond and a forest — through textbook descriptions and Activity 12.1, recording the biotic and abiotic components of each in a two-column observation table and noting how different organisms use the same habitat at different times.

roles.role_description: Introduces the two habitats using the textbook examples and guides students to set up and populate their observation tables.
Complete the observation table for each habitat, listing organisms and abiotic elements and adding a note on resource-use differences such as nocturnal versus diurnal species.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea of a habitat using the pond and forest examples, asking students to name things they would find in each.
Students independently set up and fill a two-column observation table, listing biotic organisms and abiotic components for the pond and forest habitats drawn from the chapter.
Students add a third column noting how two organisms in the same habitat use its resources differently, drawing on the nocturnal snake and diurnal rodent example.
Whole-class share-out: teacher collects two or three examples from students and draws attention to the idea that the same habitat supports many different ways of living.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit establishes the chapter's foundational vocabulary — habitat, biotic, and abiotic — before any abstraction is introduced. Watch for students who list only large, visible animals as biotic components and forget microorganisms, soil bacteria, or decomposers; prompt them with 'What else lives in the pond that you cannot see?' A useful checkpoint before moving on is whether every student's table includes at least one abiotic component that directly supports an organism's survival.
materials: Blank paper or exercise book for observation table

periods.activity_title: Who Lives Here? A Garden Census
periods.activity_description: Students conduct the quadrat census from Activity 12.2, marking a 1 m × 1 m patch in the school garden or a designated indoor equivalent, counting individuals of each plant and animal species present, and organising their counts into a population tally that distinguishes species from individuals.

roles.role_description: Explains the quadrat method, assigns groups to patches, and circulates to prompt students to distinguish between individual organisms and the species they belong to.
Mark and observe their assigned patch, count organisms by species, and record a tally table that will serve as the raw data for the next unit's discussion.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the quadrat method — how to mark a 1 m × 1 m area and why scientists count this way — linking it to the population concept introduced in Section 12.2.
Groups go to their assigned patch (or use an indoor substitute such as a potted-plant cluster) and count organisms by species, recording individual counts in a tally table.
Groups return and compile their tallies on a shared class board, noting which species appeared in more than one group's quadrat.
Teacher poses the question: 'All these different species sharing the same patch — what do we call that, and what does it tell us?' to prime the community concept for the next unit.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the previous unit's habitat vocabulary by having students generate real population data from their own environment. A common error is counting the same individual twice when it moves — advise groups to observe quietly and systematically from one corner outward. If outdoor access is not possible, the teacher may substitute a large photograph of a forest floor from the textbook and ask students to count species in a marked region of the image.
materials: String or chalk to mark quadrat boundaries

periods.activity_title: From Patch to Ecosystem: Building the Vocabulary Stack
periods.activity_description: Students use their census data from the previous unit to construct a nested hierarchy — individual, population, community, ecosystem — and formally define each level using textbook language, then classify each item from their tally into the correct level of organisation.

roles.role_description: Leads a structured explanation of the four ecological levels, using the class census data as concrete examples and introducing the formal definition of an ecosystem from Section 12.4.
Write the four-level hierarchy in their own words and classify at least six items from their census tally into the correct level, justifying each classification in one sentence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the individual-population-community-ecosystem hierarchy using the class's own census data: 'Your one grasshopper is an individual; all grasshoppers in the garden are a population; all species together form a community; add the abiotic components and you have an ecosystem.'

Teacher formally defines ecosystem (Section 12.4) and distinguishes aquatic from terrestrial types, noting that a farm is a human-made ecosystem — a concept students will revisit later in the chapter.
Students individually classify six items from their census tally into the hierarchy and write a one-sentence justification for each classification.
Pair-check: students swap books and verify each other's classifications, flagging any item they disagree on for class discussion.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit consolidates the census data into formal concepts, so begin by displaying the class tally from the previous unit prominently. A frequent confusion at this stage is between 'community' and 'ecosystem' — students often think the ecosystem is simply 'more organisms'; the key distinction is the inclusion of abiotic components, and the teacher should probe this explicitly. Asking 'Is a fish tank with no water an ecosystem?' is a productive checkpoint.
materials: Class census tally (from previous unit, on board)

periods.activity_description: Students examine a pond habitat diagram and classify each interaction they can identify into one of three categories — biotic–abiotic, abiotic–abiotic, and biotic–biotic — producing a sorted interaction table, as in Activity 12.4, and adding one original example for each category.

roles.role_description: Projects or draws the pond habitat diagram on the board, models the classification of one interaction from each category, and then withdraws to let groups work independently.
Examine the diagram, classify interactions into the three categories, and collaboratively generate one original example per category from a habitat of their choice.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models one classification: 'A fish breathes oxygen dissolved in water — that is biotic–abiotic because a living organism is responding to a non-living component.' Students copy the three-column table heading into their books.
Groups systematically work through the pond diagram, identifying and classifying interactions; they must find at least two examples for each category before adding their own.
Each group shares their original example for one category; the teacher records these on the board and the class votes on whether the classification is correct, with brief justification required.

Teacher draws attention to the abiotic–abiotic category (e.g., sunlight warming water) and explains that even non-living components shape the ecosystem — connecting to the abiotic dependence point from Section 12.4.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the classification skill introduced in the previous unit by applying it to interactions rather than organisms. Students commonly place any interaction involving a plant as biotic–abiotic rather than recognising that plant–plant competition is biotic–biotic; watch for this conflation and ask 'Are both parties in this interaction living?' as a clarifying prompt. Groups that finish early can be asked to identify one interaction in the diagram where the direction of the arrow could be reversed — a preview of the bidirectional dependence concept.
materials: Pond habitat diagram (textbook, Section 12.4, or hand-drawn on board)

periods.stage_label: Trace feeding relationships and construct food webs
periods.activity_title: Chains, Levels, and Pyramids in a Grassland
periods.activity_description: Students classify grassland organisms by feeding habit (Activity 12.5), then draw food chains among grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, and eagle (Activity 12.6), label each trophic level, and construct a trophic pyramid for a crop field food chain (Activity 12.7).

roles.role_description: Introduces producers, consumers, and trophic levels using Section 12.5 vocabulary, then sets students working through the three linked activities in sequence.
Complete the classification, draw and label food chains with trophic levels, and construct the trophic pyramid, annotating each level with the correct consumer type.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces producer, consumer (herbivore, carnivore, omnivore), and trophic level using the Section 12.5 definitions, asking students to suggest which organisms from their census data belong to each category.

Students individually classify organisms from the forest ecosystem image (Activity 12.5) and then draw at least two food chains for the grassland organisms from Activity 12.6, labelling each link with an arrow and each organism with its trophic level.
Students construct the trophic pyramid (Activity 12.7) for the crop field food chain, labelling each tier with organism name and trophic level number.

Quick whole-class review: teacher draws one food chain on the board with a deliberate error in arrow direction and asks the class to identify and correct it, reinforcing the 'energy flows from eaten to eater' convention.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the chapter's pivot from classification of components to tracing relationships — a meaningful increase in cognitive demand from the previous two units. The most persistent error at this stage is drawing food-chain arrows in the wrong direction; students often draw them from predator to prey, interpreting the arrow as 'eats' rather than 'energy passes to'. The deliberate error in the closing review is the key corrective move. If students are working at different speeds, those who finish early can be prompted to ask: 'What would happen to the eagle if all the frogs disappeared?' — a preview of cascade thinking.
materials: Ruler and pencil for pyramid diagram

periods.stage_label: Trace feeding relationships and construct food webs
periods.activity_title: Weaving the Web: Completing Missing Links
periods.activity_description: Students complete a partial food web diagram by identifying and adding missing feeding-relationship arrows (Activity 12.8), then investigate how removing one organism from the web changes the number of connections that remain, producing a written prediction and justification.

roles.role_description: Distributes or projects the partial food web, explains the task of identifying missing arrows, and poses the removal inquiry question once students have completed the diagram.
Complete the food web collaboratively, then each group selects a different organism to remove and traces which connections are lost, recording their reasoning in writing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher projects the partial food web and asks students to identify one obviously missing arrow before the group work begins, establishing the task logic.

Groups complete the food web by adding all missing arrows, ensuring each arrow points from food source to consumer, and checking that every organism has at least one incoming and one outgoing connection.

Each group selects one organism to remove from the web and traces the consequences: which organisms lose a food source, which lose a predator, and what happens to their populations — recorded as a written prediction with justification.

Two or three groups share their removal scenarios; the class discusses whether the consequences predicted make ecological sense, and the teacher connects this to the idea that food webs distribute risk across many connections.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the chain-and-pyramid work of the previous unit by showing that real feeding relationships are networked, not linear. Students sometimes add arrows randomly to complete the web rather than reasoning about which organism could realistically eat which; encourage them to ask 'Does this organism have the right body size, habitat, and diet to eat that one?' before adding a link. The removal inquiry primes the cascade-analysis thinking that will be central to the next stage.
materials: Partial food web diagram (from textbook Activity 12.8, reproduced on board or worksheet)
homework: Select one food web from the chapter and write two sentences explaining what would happen to a species of your choice if its primary food source were suddenly removed — give a reason for your prediction.

periods.stage_label: Trace feeding relationships and construct food webs
periods.activity_title: Decomposers, Nutrient Cycles, and the Closing of the Loop
periods.activity_description: Students learn about decomposers (Section 12.6) and their role in nutrient recycling, then map the pathway of nutrients from a dead plant back into the soil and up through a food chain, producing a labelled cycle diagram that connects decomposition to the food web constructed in the previous unit.

roles.role_description: Presents the decomposer concept, explains decomposition as nutrient recycling, and uses the mushroom-on-dead-tree and dung-beetle examples to anchor the concept before students construct the cycle diagram.
Draw and label a nutrient cycle diagram that starts with a dead organism, passes through decomposers, returns nutrients to soil, and connects back into a food chain from the previous unit.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces decomposers and the concept of decomposition as nature's recycling system, using the mushroom and dung-beetle examples from Section 12.6 and asking students where the nutrients in a dead leaf eventually go.

Students individually draw a nutrient cycle diagram: dead organism → decomposers (fungi, bacteria) → nutrients released into soil → absorbed by plants → eaten by consumers — labelling each arrow with the process occurring.

Students add a dashed box around the decomposer step in their diagram and annotate it with two examples from the chapter (mushroom on dead tree; beetles and flies on dung), then write one sentence explaining why 'nothing is truly wasted in nature.'
Teacher connects the cycle back to the food web: 'Every dead organism in your web from last unit eventually passes through this loop — decomposers are the invisible link that keeps the web running.'

periods.teacher_notes: Decomposers are frequently omitted from students' mental models of ecosystems because they are invisible — students often assume nutrients 'just disappear' when organisms die. The key misconception to challenge here is that decomposers are not consumers in the food-chain sense; they are a separate functional group that closes the nutrient loop. Connecting the cycle diagram explicitly to the food web from the previous unit makes the relationship concrete rather than abstract.

periods.stage_label: Explain inter-organism relationships and ecosystem balance
periods.activity_title: Partnerships, Parasites, and Competitors: Mapping Who Benefits
periods.activity_description: Students examine the four inter-organism relationship types — competition, mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism — from Section 12.8, classify each textbook example using a benefits matrix (+/0/−), and then generate one original example from their local environment for each relationship type, justifying the classification.

roles.role_description: Introduces the four relationship types and the benefits matrix (+/0/−) framework, models one classification using the honeybee–flower example, and then sets groups to work.
Classify all textbook examples using the matrix, then generate and justify one local example per relationship type, sharing their most debated classification with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces competition, mutualism, commensalism, and parasitism using the framework: 'Who benefits (+), who is unaffected (0), and who is harmed (−)?' and models the honeybee–flower pair as mutualism (+/+).

Groups classify the remaining textbook examples — orchid on tree branch (commensalism), tick on dog (parasitism), two plants competing for sunlight (competition) — using the matrix, then brainstorm one local example for each type.
Groups share their most debated classification; the class discusses whether the proposed relationship is correctly assigned and what evidence would confirm it.

Teacher connects the relationship types to ecosystem balance: 'Each of these relationships is part of what keeps populations from growing without limit — together they make the balance dynamic rather than fixed.'

periods.teacher_notes: This unit introduces a qualitatively different kind of relationship from the feeding relationships in the previous stage — these are not about energy transfer but about mutual effects on survival and population size. Students frequently confuse commensalism with mutualism because they assume any two organisms sharing a space must both benefit; the orchid–tree example is critical here because the tree is genuinely unaffected. Ask groups to explain what 'unaffected' means in measurable terms to sharpen the distinction.
materials: Exercise book for benefits matrix table

periods.stage_label: Explain inter-organism relationships and ecosystem balance
periods.activity_title: The Fish Pond Study: Reading a Real Cascade
periods.activity_description: Students read and analyse the two-pond research study from Section 12.3 and Activity 12.3, tracing the indirect cascade from fish introduction through dragonfly depletion, pollinator increase, and seed production gain, and producing a labelled cascade diagram that maps each cause-and-effect link.

roles.role_description: Sets the reading task and provides a blank cascade template with labelled boxes for students to fill, prompting students to explain the direction of each effect before moving to the next link.

Read the study, trace the sequence of consequences, complete the cascade diagram with labelled arrows, and write a concluding sentence explaining how a change in one biotic component can reach an abiotic outcome.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the two-pond scenario: 'One pond has fish, the other does not — how could that single difference end up affecting seed production in plants on the bank?' Students make a quick written prediction before reading.

Students read the study independently and complete the cascade diagram: fish introduced → dragonfly larvae eaten → fewer dragonflies → more bees and butterflies → greater pollination → higher seed production, labelling each arrow with the mechanism.

Students write a concluding sentence connecting the study to the ecosystem definition from Section 12.4: explaining how a single biotic change produced both biotic and abiotic consequences across the system.

Teacher debriefs the predictions from the opening: 'Who was surprised by the direction of the effect? What made it hard to predict?' — surfacing the concept of indirect effects as the key idea to carry forward.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit uses a real research study to make the cascade concept concrete before students encounter the more complex disruption examples in the next stage. Students often read the pond study as a simple linear story and miss that it crosses multiple ecological levels — biotic to biotic to abiotic; prompt them to ask 'What kind of component changed at each step?' as they fill the diagram. The opening prediction task is important: if students revise their predictions after reading, that revision is itself evidence of learning.
materials: Blank cascade diagram template (hand-drawn or teacher-prepared on board)

periods.stage_label: Analyse cascading disruptions and evaluate ecosystem consequences
periods.activity_title: When One Thread Breaks: Analysing the Frog-Leg Export Case
periods.activity_description: Students read the frog-leg export case study from Activity 12.9 and the pond pollution cascade from Section 12.7, trace each cascade chain in full, and evaluate the consequences at each step — distinguishing ecological, agricultural, and human health effects — then propose what intervention at which step would have broken the chain most effectively.

roles.role_description: Introduces both disruption scenarios, provides a structured analysis table for students to complete, and facilitates the class discussion on intervention choices.
Trace each cascade in the analysis table, evaluate consequences at each node, and collaboratively argue for the most effective intervention point, presenting their reasoning to the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly presents both disruption scenarios — pond pollution and frog-leg export — and asks students to identify which type of disruption (natural or human-made) each represents before reading.

Groups complete the analysis table for both cascades: recording the initial disruption, each subsequent effect, the type of component affected at each step, and the ultimate consequence for the ecosystem and for humans.

Each group selects one cascade and argues for a specific intervention point — stating at which step in the chain an action would have prevented the most downstream harm and why — then presents their choice in two sentences to the class.

Class discusses: 'Was the government's ban on frog-leg export an ecological response or a human welfare response — or both?' — pushing students to recognise that ecosystem disruptions have consequences that cross ecological and social boundaries.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is the chapter's analytical core: students must now reason about causation across multiple steps rather than simply tracing a known chain. The most common error is choosing the intervention point that is easiest to imagine (banning pesticides) rather than the one that is most ecologically upstream (protecting frog populations); push groups to justify why their chosen point prevents more consequences than a later one. The closing discussion question is deliberately ambiguous — there is no single correct answer, and productive disagreement between groups is the goal.
materials: Analysis table template (drawn on board or in exercise book)
homework: Write two sentences: identify one ecosystem disruption from your own locality and trace at least two downstream effects it might produce — be specific about which component is affected at each step.

periods.stage_label: Analyse cascading disruptions and evaluate ecosystem consequences
periods.activity_title: The Sundarbans and the Green Revolution: Ecosystems Under Pressure
periods.activity_description: Students examine the Sundarbans case study (Section 12.9) and the Green Revolution's ecological costs (Section 12.9.2) to identify the specific ecosystem relationships that are being disrupted in each case and evaluate whether the disruptions share common patterns, producing a comparative analysis with evidence from both cases.

roles.role_description: Frames the two cases as real-world applications of the cascade and relationship concepts built across the chapter, and poses the comparative analysis question to guide group investigation.
Read both case sections, identify the specific relationships being disrupted in each, and produce a written comparative analysis that names at least two shared disruption patterns and one difference.

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the Sundarbans briefly — world's largest mangrove forest, UNESCO World Heritage Site, now threatened — and asks: 'Based on everything we have traced in this chapter, what kinds of relationships do you expect are being disrupted there?'

Groups read Sections 12.9 and 12.9.2 and complete a two-column analysis: 'Sundarbans' and 'Green Revolution farming' — identifying the relationships disrupted (biotic–biotic, biotic–abiotic), the cascading consequences, and whether organic or natural farming could interrupt any of the chains they identified.

Groups write two to three sentences identifying shared disruption patterns — for example, both cases involve the breaking of a biotic–abiotic relationship that then cascades into further biotic disruption — and one way the two cases differ.

Whole-class debrief: teacher asks one group to state a shared pattern and another to challenge or extend it, consolidating the idea that ecosystem disruption follows recognisable patterns regardless of the specific habitat.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the final unit of the taught arc before the synthesis, so it should leave students holding the chapter's central analytical insight: disruptions to ecological relationships follow patterns that can be recognised and reasoned about. Students may focus narrowly on deforestation as the single cause in the Sundarbans case and miss the compounding effects of illegal hunting and industrial pollution — prompt them to identify at least two separate relationship types being disrupted simultaneously. The comparative structure is important: students who can name a shared pattern across two different ecosystems are demonstrating the analysis that the chapter's dissolution test targets.
materials: Two-column analysis table in exercise book

periods.stage_label: Analyse cascading disruptions and evaluate ecosystem consequences

roles.role_description: Frames the synthesis task, provides a blank ecosystem relationship map template, and circulates to challenge students to make cross-concept connections they have not yet articulated explicitly.

Construct the relationship map integrating all chapter concepts, then use it to evaluate the disruption scenario in writing, tracing at least three linked consequences with named relationship types at each step.

periods.activity_title: The Mangrove Shoreline: Reading a New Ecosystem Whole
periods.activity_description: Students receive a profile card describing a coastal mangrove creek — a setting not used anywhere in the chapter — that includes a sketch map, a short species list with feeding notes, and three abiotic measurements taken before and after a nearby shrimp farm was built. Working in pairs, they annotate the profile to classify every relationship shown, construct a food web from the species list, identify which decomposer role is represented, and then trace the two-step cascade that follows one specific abiotic change recorded on the card. The pair's completed annotation sheet becomes the record of the chapter drawn together in a single, unfamiliar place.
periods.teacher_notes: This unit asks pairs to annotate an unfamiliar mangrove creek profile card so that every chapter concept — from habitat and trophic level to mutualism and cascade — does visible work in a single place. The critical facilitation move is circulating during the annotation phase and asking, 'If this relationship changed, which other arrow on your sheet would change next?' to push students from labelling interactions in isolation toward genuine cross-concept synthesis. Full card content and the abiotic data table are ready to print (see materials).
materials: One mangrove creek profile card per pair, A4 teacher-prepared (see visual aid: 'Mangrove creek profile card')
Abiotic data table printed on the profile card (see visual aid: 'Before/after abiotic data table')
One legend strip per pair (see visual aid: 'Interaction-type legend strip')
Coloured pens or pencils in at least three colours (one per interaction category: biotic–biotic, biotic–abiotic, abiotic–abiotic)

time_bands.activity: Teacher distributes the profile cards face-up and gives pairs two minutes to read silently. Teacher then asks the class: 'Without writing anything yet — what kind of place is this, and what living and non-living things does it contain?' Two or three pairs share aloud. Teacher confirms the habitat framing and states the task: 'Your job is to annotate this card so that everything it shows is classified and connected. By the end, your card should look like the whole chapter happened here.'

Pairs annotate the species list and sketch map for interactions. Using the three colours, they draw and label arrows between organisms and between organisms and abiotic components, writing the relationship type beside each arrow (e.g., 'biotic–biotic / predation', 'mutualism', 'decomposer → soil nutrients → mangrove tree'). They also construct a food web by arranging the species in feeding order and connecting them with arrows, labelling each trophic level. Teacher circulates, prompting pairs who have labelled interactions in isolation to ask which arrow would change if the one they are looking at changed.

Pairs turn to the abiotic data table. Each pair selects one abiotic change shown in the before/after columns and traces a two-step cascade on the card: Step 1 — how that abiotic change affects one biotic component (labelling the interaction type); Step 2 — how that biotic change affects another organism or abiotic component further along. They record their cascade as two connected arrows added to the sketch map, each arrow annotated with the mechanism. Teacher checks that both arrows are mechanistically labelled, not just directional.

Whole-class share: teacher asks two pairs with different chosen abiotic changes to describe their two-step cascades aloud while the rest of the class checks their own annotation for the same chain. Class discusses whether the two cascades interact — if silt increases and oxygen drops, do the consequences compound or stay separate? Teacher draws both cascades on the board as a combined web, showing that the ecosystem's response is not a single chain but an interconnected set of responses.

Teacher closes by reading aloud the chapter's central ideas — habitat, biotic and abiotic components, population, community, ecosystem, food chain, food web, trophic level, decomposers, the five relationship types, cascade, ecosystem services — and after each one asks: 'Where did this appear on your card?' Pairs point to or tap the relevant annotation. The final statement is not a summary but an observation: the mangrove creek card required every one of these ideas to be read correctly, which is what it means for an ecosystem to work as a system.

visual_aids.title: Mangrove creek profile card
visual_aids.text:
Print or hand-draw on a single A4 sheet. The card contains three elements:

1. LABELLED SKETCH MAP — a creek shoreline showing open water, mudflat, and fringing mangrove trees, with space for students to draw and annotate arrows between organisms and abiotic components.

2. SPECIES LIST WITH FEEDING NOTES —
• Mangrove trees — producers; fix energy through photosynthesis; shed leaf litter continuously
• Mangrove fungi — decomposers; break down leaf litter and dead organic matter into soil nutrients
• Fiddler crabs — detritivores/omnivores; consume leaf litter and algae; burrow in mud
• Mudskippers — carnivores; prey on fiddler crabs and mosquito larvae
• Herons — carnivores; prey on mudskippers and fiddler crabs
• Mosquito larvae — consumers; feed on organic particles in water
• Sunbirds — mutualism partner with flowering mangrove plants; feed on nectar, carry pollen

3. ABIOTIC DATA TABLE — see visual aid: 'Before/after abiotic data table'.

Design note: the card should leave clear annotation space around the sketch map and beside each species entry so pairs can draw coloured arrows and write relationship-type labels directly on the sheet.

visual_aids.title: Before/after abiotic data table
visual_aids.table:
Abiotic factor | Before shrimp farm | After shrimp farm
Dissolved oxygen | 7.2 mg/L | 4.1 mg/L
Silt level | Low (clear water) | High (turbid water)

visual_aids.title: Cascade reasoning guide (teacher reference)
visual_aids.text:
Students select ONE abiotic change from the before/after table and trace a two-step cascade. The following example based on increased silt is recommended for clarity, but students may choose any change:

Example cascade (silt):
— Step 1 (abiotic → biotic): Increased silt raises water turbidity, reducing sunlight penetration, which reduces photosynthesis in mangrove trees.
— Step 2 (biotic → biotic): Reduced photosynthesis means less leaf litter falls; this reduces food available to mangrove fungi (decomposers) and fiddler crabs (detritivores), lowering their populations.

Each step must be recorded as an annotated arrow on the sketch map with the mechanism written beside it (not just the direction). Both cascades shared in the whole-class phase (minutes 32–40) should be drawn on the board together so students can see whether the consequences compound.

visual_aids.title: Interaction-type legend strip
visual_aids.text: Print one per pair as a narrow strip (can be cut from the bottom of the profile card sheet).

visual_aids.title: Colour code for arrows
visual_aids.table:
Colour | Interaction type
1 | Biotic–biotic interaction
2 | Biotic–abiotic interaction
3 | Abiotic–abiotic interaction

visual_aids.title: Relationship types to label
visual_aids.table:
Relationship | Meaning
Predation / herbivory | One organism eats another
Mutualism | Both organisms benefit
Commensalism | One benefits, one unaffected
Parasitism | One benefits, one harmed
Competition | Both organisms compete for the same resource
Decomposer role | Breaks down dead matter, releases nutrients to abiotic environment

visual_aids.title: Trophic level reminder
visual_aids.text: A trophic level is a feeding position in a food chain. Producers are Level 1; primary consumers (eat producers) are Level 2; secondary consumers (eat primary consumers) are Level 3; and so on.

visual_aids.title: Closing chapter-concept checklist (teacher reference)
visual_aids.text:
During the closing band, read each term aloud and ask pairs: 'Where did this appear on your card?' Terms to name in sequence:
habitat · biotic components · abiotic components · population · community · ecosystem · food chain · food web · trophic level · decomposer · mutualism · commensalism · parasitism · competition · cascade · ecosystem services

The closing statement is not a summary but an observation: the mangrove creek card required every one of these ideas to be read correctly, which is what it means for an ecosystem to work as a system.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students explore two contrasting habitats, record biotic and abiotic components, and conduct a quadrat census to generate real population data from their own environment.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and list the biotic and abiotic components of a given habitat and distinguish between an individual organism and the population and community it belongs to.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct the individual–population–community–ecosystem hierarchy from census data and classify interactions in a pond habitat into biotic–abiotic, abiotic–abiotic, and biotic–biotic categories.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can correctly classify organisms and interactions into the four-level ecological hierarchy and distinguish between the three types of biotic–abiotic–abiotic interactions in a habitat diagram.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Trace feeding relationships and construct food webs
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify organisms by feeding habit, draw food chains with labelled trophic levels, complete a food web by adding missing arrows, investigate the consequences of removing one organism, and map the decomposer nutrient cycle.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct a food web from a set of organisms, label trophic levels correctly, and explain how decomposers close the nutrient cycle within the food web.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain inter-organism relationships and ecosystem balance
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students classify mutualism, commensalism, parasitism, and competition using a benefits matrix, generate local examples, and trace the indirect cascade in the two-pond fish study to explain how a single biotic change affects other biotic and abiotic components.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain how the four types of inter-organism relationships contribute to ecosystem balance and trace an indirect cascade from a single biotic change through multiple ecological levels.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Analyse cascading disruptions and evaluate ecosystem consequences
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse the frog-leg export and pond pollution cascades, evaluate intervention points, compare disruption patterns in the Sundarbans and Green Revolution cases, and synthesise all chapter concepts into an ecosystem relationship map applied to a novel disruption scenario.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can analyse patterns of ecological relationships between living organisms and their environments by tracing how disruptions to biotic and abiotic components propagate as cascading consequences across an ecosystem, and can evaluate which relationships are broken at each step.

assessment_items.question_text: A student walks through a forest and notices sunlight filtering through the leaves, a deer grazing, a stream running over rocks, and several mushrooms growing on a fallen log. Which of the following lists contains only abiotic components of this habitat?

options.label: A
options.text: Mushrooms, rocks, and sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: Stream water, fallen log, and deer

options.label: C
options.text: Sunlight, deer, and stream water

options.label: D
options.text: Sunlight, stream water, and rocks

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option indicates the student has not distinguished living organisms from non-living components — placing 'deer' (a living organism) in the abiotic list shows the biotic/abiotic boundary has not been internalised.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option indicates the student has misclassified mushrooms (living decomposers, therefore biotic) as abiotic, a common confusion because mushrooms are not obviously animal or plant.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option indicates the student treats 'fallen log' as abiotic simply because it is no longer alive; this reveals a misconception about the boundary — a fallen log is derived from a once-living organism and is classified as biotic material in ecosystem contexts, while 'deer' is clearly biotic.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the written scenario may be supported by a simple two-column sorting task (biotic / abiotic) using picture cards of the same items before attempting the MCQ. Students who find the question straightforward can be asked to identify one additional abiotic component not mentioned in the scenario.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Level | Description | Example from a pond
Individual | One single organism of one species | One catfish
Population | All organisms of the same species in one habitat | All catfish in the pond
Community | All populations of all species in one habitat | Catfish + frogs + water lilies + algae
Ecosystem | Community plus all abiotic components | Catfish + frogs + water lilies + algae + water + sunlight + mud
assessment_items.question_text: A researcher counts 47 frogs, 12 water snakes, and thousands of algae cells living together in a pond. She notes the pond also has water, sunlight, and mud. Refer to the table provided. Which term correctly describes all the frogs in the pond — and only the frogs?

options.label: A
options.text: A community

options.label: B
options.text: A habitat

options.label: C
options.text: A population

options.label: D
options.text: An ecosystem

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'community' reveals that the student has not retained the species-specificity requirement — a community includes multiple species, but the question asks about one species only.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'ecosystem' suggests the student is using 'ecosystem' as a general term for 'everything in the pond' without recognising that it requires both biotic and abiotic components and covers all species together.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'habitat' indicates the student has confused the place where organisms live with the organisms themselves — habitat refers to the physical environment, not the organisms that occupy it.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the hierarchy may benefit from drawing the four nested levels as concentric circles and placing the frogs on the diagram before answering. Students who answer correctly quickly can be asked to write which term would describe all frogs plus all snakes plus all algae together.

assessment_items.question_text: In a pond habitat, plant roots hold the mud in place and prevent it from washing away, while sunlight warms the surface water and causes some water to evaporate. Which row correctly identifies the type of each interaction?

options.label: A
options.text: Plant roots holding mud: abiotic–abiotic; sunlight warming water: abiotic–abiotic

options.label: B
options.text: Plant roots holding mud: biotic–abiotic; sunlight warming water: abiotic–abiotic

options.label: C
options.text: Plant roots holding mud: biotic–abiotic; sunlight warming water: biotic–abiotic

options.label: D
options.text: Plant roots holding mud: biotic–biotic; sunlight warming water: biotic–abiotic

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the student has classified 'plant roots + mud' as biotic–biotic, suggesting they have failed to recognise that mud/soil is an abiotic component — a confusion between the organism and its substrate.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the student has classified plant roots as abiotic, indicating the biotic/abiotic boundary for plants has not been secured despite the Stage 1 work.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the student correctly identified the first interaction but misclassified sunlight warming water as biotic–abiotic, suggesting they inserted a living organism into an interaction that involves only two abiotic components.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the written description may be helped by underlining each participant in the interaction and labelling it B (biotic) or A (abiotic) before deciding the interaction type. Students who finish quickly can be asked to generate one example of the third interaction type (biotic–biotic) that could also occur in a pond.

assessment_items.question_text: A textbook states: 'Plants release oxygen into the air, and their roots prevent soil erosion.' A student says this proves that abiotic components depend on biotic components, not just the other way around. Which statement best evaluates this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The student is correct — the interaction shows a biotic component (plants) directly influencing two abiotic components (air composition and soil stability).

options.label: B
options.text: The student is incorrect — oxygen in the air is an abiotic component that existed before plants evolved, so plants cannot be said to influence it.

options.label: C
options.text: The student is incorrect — plants only receive from abiotic components such as sunlight and water; they do not affect abiotic components.

options.label: D
options.text: The student is partially correct — plants affect only soil, not air, because oxygen is itself a biotic product.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a persistent one-directional model of biotic–abiotic relationships — the student believes only abiotic components influence biotic ones, not the reverse, which is the very misconception Section 12.4 is designed to correct.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a partial misconception: the student accepts that biotic components influence soil (a visible, tangible abiotic element) but rejects the influence on air because of a confusion between the abiotic category 'air' and the biological process of oxygen production.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a historical reasoning error — the fact that oxygen pre-existed plants is irrelevant to whether plants currently influence atmospheric oxygen levels; the student is confusing evolutionary origin with present-day interaction.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the evaluative framing difficult may first be asked simply to list the abiotic components that the plants in the statement are affecting, before judging whether the student's claim is correct. Advanced students can be asked to provide a second example from the chapter of a biotic component influencing an abiotic one.

assessment_items.question_text: A student examining a forest ecosystem diagram identifies the following interactions: (1) a deer eating grass, (2) wind dispersing seeds, (3) tree roots absorbing water from the soil. Classify each interaction as biotic–biotic, abiotic–abiotic, or biotic–abiotic. For each, name both participants and state which is biotic and which is abiotic (where relevant).
expected_elements: Interaction 1 (deer eating grass) correctly classified as biotic–biotic, with both deer and grass named as biotic organisms.
Interaction 2 (wind dispersing seeds) correctly classified as abiotic–biotic (or biotic–abiotic), with wind named as abiotic and seeds/plant named as biotic.
Interaction 3 (tree roots absorbing water) correctly classified as biotic–abiotic, with tree roots named as biotic and soil water named as abiotic.
Each classification includes a one-phrase justification naming which component is biotic or abiotic.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the written classification difficult may use a two-column labelling step first — writing 'B' or 'A' above each participant in the interaction — before assigning the category. Students who complete the task quickly can be asked to draw a fourth interaction of the abiotic–abiotic type from the same forest ecosystem and justify their choice.

assessment_items.question_text: In a grassland food chain — grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle — a student labels the frog as a 'primary consumer.' A second student disagrees and says the frog is a secondary consumer. Which student is correct, and why?

options.label: A
options.text: Both students are correct — 'primary consumer' and 'secondary consumer' are interchangeable terms for any animal that eats another animal.

options.label: B
options.text: Neither student is correct — the frog is an omnivore and therefore does not occupy a fixed trophic level.

options.label: C
options.text: The first student is correct — the frog is the first animal in the chain that eats another animal, so it is the primary consumer.

options.label: D
options.text: The second student is correct — the frog eats grasshoppers, which already ate grass, making the frog a secondary consumer at trophic level 3.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the student is numbering consumer levels by the order of animal appearance in the chain rather than by the number of feeding steps from the producer — a systematic misapplication of the trophic level concept.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the student has not internalised that trophic levels are positional and relational — they are not generic labels for all animals but specific positions in a feeding hierarchy.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a category error: the student has confused the frog's diet type (carnivore in this chain — it eats grasshoppers) with the omnivore category, and further incorrectly inferred that diet flexibility means no fixed trophic level.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain may benefit from numbering each organism in the chain (1 = grass, 2 = grasshopper, 3 = frog…) before assigning consumer levels. Students who find this straightforward can be asked to predict what happens to the snake's trophic level if the food chain is extended with a new top predator.

assessment_items.question_text: After all organisms in a forest food web die, fungi and bacteria begin breaking down their bodies. Which statement most accurately describes the role of these decomposers in keeping the ecosystem functional?

options.label: A
options.text: Decomposers act as top consumers in the food web, occupying the highest trophic level and completing the food chain.

options.label: B
options.text: Decomposers compete with producers for sunlight and soil space, which keeps the ecosystem in balance by limiting plant growth.

options.label: C
options.text: Decomposers produce oxygen through decomposition, which replaces the oxygen that organisms consumed while they were alive.

options.label: D
options.text: Decomposers release nutrients locked in dead matter back into the soil, making them available to producers and restarting the nutrient cycle.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the student has assimilated decomposers into the food-chain model as a consumer tier rather than recognising them as a separate functional category that operates outside the linear chain.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a confusion between decomposition and photosynthesis — the student has attributed oxygen production to decomposers rather than to producers, conflating two very different biochemical processes.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a vague sense that decomposers 'do something to control the ecosystem' but applies it as competition with producers — an invented relationship not present in the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the decomposer role can be asked to trace one nutrient (e.g., nitrogen in a dead leaf) step by step before answering. Students with strong understanding can be asked to explain why removing all decomposers from a food web would eventually cause producers to decline even if no producer was directly harmed.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Organism | Eats | Eaten by
Crop plants | Sunlight and soil nutrients | Caterpillar, Locust
Caterpillar | Crop plants | Frog, Sparrow
Locust | Crop plants | Sparrow, Lizard
Frog | Caterpillar | Snake
Sparrow | Caterpillar, Locust | Hawk
Lizard | Locust | Snake, Hawk
Snake | Frog, Lizard | Hawk
Hawk | Sparrow, Lizard, Snake | —
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Using the information in the table, draw a food web for this crop field ecosystem and label the trophic level of each organism. Then explain in one sentence what would happen to the hawk population if all frogs and lizards were removed from the ecosystem.
expected_elements: A correctly drawn food web with arrows pointing from food source to consumer for all relationships listed in the table.
Crop plants correctly labelled as producers (trophic level 1).
Caterpillar and locust correctly labelled as primary consumers (trophic level 2).
Frog, sparrow, and lizard correctly labelled as secondary consumers (trophic level 3).
Snake correctly labelled as a tertiary consumer (trophic level 4) with multiple prey connections shown.
Hawk correctly labelled at the top of the web.
A sentence explaining that hawk population would decline because two of its indirect food sources (frog and lizard) are removed, reducing the available prey (snake and lizard routes).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to draw the complete web may first draw all linear chains separately (e.g., crop → caterpillar → frog → snake → hawk) and then identify shared nodes before integrating them. Students who complete the task quickly can be asked to identify which organism's removal would most severely disconnect the food web and justify their choice.

assessment_items.question_text: An orchid grows on the branch of a tall tree. The orchid benefits by gaining access to sunlight high above the forest floor. The tree neither gains nor loses anything from the orchid's presence. A student claims this is an example of mutualism because 'both organisms are involved.' Which response best evaluates the student's claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The claim is correct — any relationship involving two organisms is mutualism because both are participating in the interaction.

options.label: B
options.text: The claim is partially correct — it is mutualism only when the orchid is in flower, because then the tree gains pollinators from insects visiting the orchid.

options.label: C
options.text: The claim is wrong — this is commensalism, not mutualism, because only the orchid benefits; mutualism requires both organisms to benefit.

options.label: D
options.text: The claim is wrong — this is parasitism, not mutualism, because the orchid takes something (branch space) from the tree without the tree's consent.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the student has reduced mutualism to 'two organisms interacting' — stripping the concept of its defining criterion (mutual benefit) and conflating participation with benefit.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals the student is attempting to reason about the relationship but introduces an imagined indirect benefit (pollinator attraction) not present in the scenario — a plausible-sounding but unsupported inference.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a confusion between commensalism and parasitism: the student interprets 'taking something' as inherently harmful, but parasitism requires measurable harm to the host, not merely use of space.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the three-way distinction difficult can be directed to apply the +/0/− matrix explicitly: 'Score each organism in this interaction +, 0, or − and use the pattern to name the relationship.' Students who answer correctly can be asked to rewrite the scenario so that it becomes genuine mutualism and explain what would need to change.

assessment_items.question_text: In the two-pond research study, introducing fish into a pond led — through a cascade of interactions — to increased seed production in plants on the bank. Which sequence correctly traces this cascade?

options.label: A
options.text: Fish eat bees and butterflies → fewer pollinators → plants compensate by producing more seeds to ensure survival

options.label: B
options.text: Fish eat dragonfly larvae → fewer adult dragonflies → more bees and butterflies → greater pollination → more seeds produced

options.label: C
options.text: Fish eat dragonfly larvae → fewer dragonflies → dragonflies no longer eat bees and butterflies → bees and butterflies increase → more seeds produced

options.label: D
options.text: Fish eat plant roots underwater → fewer aquatic plants → more sunlight reaches bank → more flowering plants → more seeds produced

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the student constructed a plausible-sounding but entirely invented cascade — fish eating plant roots is not described in the study; this shows the student is generating a logical chain without anchoring it in the textbook evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals a misreading of the predator chain — the student has placed fish as a direct predator of pollinators, collapsing the dragonfly intermediate step and misunderstanding the indirect nature of the cascade.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option is a near-miss: the student correctly identifies the first and last steps but introduces an error in the mechanism — dragonflies prey on insects including bees, but the specific mechanism in the study is that fewer dragonflies left more bees/butterflies alive, not that dragonflies stopped eating bees because of fish. This reveals incomplete reading of the indirect mechanism.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find multi-step sequences difficult can be asked to draw a simple arrow diagram first — placing each organism in a box and drawing arrows — before selecting the option whose text matches their diagram. Students who answer correctly can be asked to identify at which step in the sequence a biotic–abiotic interaction occurs.

assessment_items.question_text: In a grassland ecosystem, honeybees pollinate wildflowers, and ticks feed on the blood of cattle grazing in the same grassland. (a) Name the type of inter-organism relationship in each case. (b) For each relationship, state which organism benefits (+), which is unaffected (0), and which is harmed (−). (c) Explain in one sentence how losing the honeybee population would affect the grassland ecosystem's balance.
expected_elements: Honeybee–flower relationship correctly named as mutualism.
Correct benefits matrix for mutualism: honeybee (+) and flower/plant (+).
Tick–cattle relationship correctly named as parasitism.
Correct benefits matrix for parasitism: tick (+) and cattle (−).

A sentence explaining that losing honeybees would reduce pollination, leading to fewer seeds and fewer wildflowers, which would reduce the food and habitat available to other organisms that depend on wildflowers.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find part (c) difficult may be prompted with: 'What does the honeybee do for the flower, and what does the flower do for other organisms?' to help them chain the consequence. Students who complete all three parts quickly can be asked to identify what type of relationship would emerge between two plant species competing for the same pollinators.

assessment_items.question_text: In the 1980s, India exported large quantities of frog legs, which dramatically reduced frog populations in agricultural regions. Which sequence of cascading consequences did this trigger?

options.label: A
options.text: Fewer frogs → fewer tadpoles → algae in ponds increased unchecked → oxygen in pond water decreased → fish died

options.label: B
options.text: Fewer frogs → insect pest populations increased → farmers used more synthetic pesticides → further ecological and human health harm

options.label: C
options.text: Fewer frogs → more water available in ponds → fish populations increased → fish ate more insect larvae → pest populations declined

options.label: D
options.text: Fewer frogs → snake populations increased → snakes ate more rodents → rodent damage to crops decreased → farmers used fewer pesticides

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the student has invented a plausible alternative cascade — reasoning logically but not from the textbook evidence; this is a productive reasoning failure that shows the student can chain consequences but has not anchored to the specific study.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the student has tried to reverse the harm — constructing a cascade that produces a positive agricultural outcome — showing chain-reasoning ability but a failure to apply the chapter's actual evidence.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the student has used the correct starting point (fewer frogs) but has followed the chain in an aquatic direction, focusing on tadpoles and algae rather than the terrestrial agricultural consequence described in the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be guided to ask 'What did frogs eat?' and 'What happened to those organisms when frogs were gone?' as a scaffold before selecting the option. Students who answer correctly can be asked to identify the single intervention that would have broken the chain most effectively and give a reason.

assessment_items.question_text: The Green Revolution increased food production but caused long-term ecological costs including soil degradation, loss of soil microorganisms, and reduction of pollinators through monoculture. A policy adviser argues: 'The ecological costs are an acceptable trade-off because food production is more important.' Which response most effectively challenges this argument using ecological reasoning from the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument ignores that the ecological costs themselves reduce food production in the long run — loss of soil microorganisms reduces soil fertility, and loss of pollinators reduces crop yield, eventually reversing the gains.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is acceptable because human food needs are more important than ecosystem balance, and technology can always replace natural processes.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is wrong because the Sundarbans, which is not a farming ecosystem, was also harmed by industrial pollution — proving that food production is never worth the cost.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument should be rejected because the Green Revolution also harmed farmers financially, which is a more important concern than ecology.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals the student has accepted the trade-off framing without applying any ecological reasoning — they have not used the chapter's cascade logic to interrogate the claim that the costs are separable from the benefits.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the student is reasoning from a social or economic concern rather than from ecological relationships — while not incorrect as a value, it does not constitute an ecological challenge to the argument as the question asks.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the student can name a relevant chapter example (Sundarbans) but has made a logical leap — using a different ecosystem's harm as evidence against farming trade-offs — without connecting the two through the cascade reasoning the question requires.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the evaluative format difficult can be guided to first identify which ecological relationships are harmed by the Green Revolution practices, and then ask 'Do these harmed relationships also affect food production?' Students who answer correctly can be asked to extend their reasoning: 'What specific change in farming practice would interrupt the cascade of harm while still supporting food production?'

assessment_items.question_text: The Sundarbans mangrove ecosystem is being disrupted by deforestation, illegal hunting, and industrial pollution simultaneously. Using your understanding of how biotic and abiotic components interact and how disruptions cascade through ecosystems, explain: (a) which type of ecological relationship is broken first by each of the three disruptions; (b) how each broken relationship then triggers at least one further consequence in the ecosystem; and (c) which of the three disruptions you judge to be most damaging to the ecosystem's long-term balance, and why.
look_for: Deforestation correctly identified as primarily breaking a biotic–abiotic relationship (trees stabilising soil, regulating water, providing habitat) and a biotic–biotic relationship (habitat loss for animals).
Illegal hunting correctly identified as breaking a biotic–biotic relationship (removing predators or prey from food webs or reducing mutualistic/competitive relationships).
Industrial pollution correctly identified as breaking a biotic–abiotic relationship (contaminating water and soil that organisms depend on).
At least one further consequence traced for each disruption — e.g., deforestation → soil erosion → reduced soil fertility → fewer producers → cascading food web disruption.
A reasoned judgement on the most damaging disruption that references the breadth or irreversibility of the cascade it triggers, not merely an assertion.
Use of ecological vocabulary from the chapter (biotic, abiotic, food web, cascade, ecosystem balance, producers, consumers) in the reasoning.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who find part (c) difficult — making a judgement — can be guided to ask 'Which disruption affects the most relationships at once?' or 'Which is hardest to reverse once it has begun?' before committing to an answer. Students who respond fully to all three parts can be asked to propose one specific conservation action for the Sundarbans and explain which broken relationship it would most directly restore.

assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Three ecosystem disruption scenarios are described in the table. For each scenario: (1) identify the first relationship broken and name its type (biotic–biotic, biotic–abiotic, or abiotic–abiotic); (2) state whether the component most immediately affected is biotic or abiotic; (3) trace the second and third cascading consequences; and (4) name the relationship type broken at the third step. Then, below the table, write two to three sentences comparing the pattern of consequences across the three scenarios — identifying one thing all three cascades have in common and one way they differ.
assessment_items.scaffold: Fill each row of the table by moving left to right: name the first broken relationship → identify the affected component type → trace what happens next → trace the step after that → name the relationship type at that final step. After completing all three rows, look across the table to find a shared pattern and a difference.
format_of_output: A completed table with all five columns filled for all three disruption scenarios.
Two to three sentences of comparative analysis below the table identifying one shared pattern and one difference across the three cascades.

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Classification or sorting task with justification
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The classification-with-justification format is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this stage's implied LO because it requires students to apply their understanding of relationship types to novel disruption scenarios and then articulate the logic of the cascade across multiple steps — directly evidencing the analysis the dissolution test targets.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can apply the three-category interaction classification (biotic–biotic, biotic–abiotic, abiotic–abiotic) to novel disruption contexts, trace cascading consequences across at least three steps, and abstract a pattern from multiple cascades — the core analytical operation of the chapter.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to move left-to-right across the table one column at a time, preventing them from jumping to later consequences before securing the first disruption. The comparative sentences below the table are the highest-demand element: they require cross-scenario abstraction, not just row completion. Teachers should treat the comparison as the primary assessment signal — a student who completes all rows but cannot identify a shared pattern has demonstrated classification but not analysis.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses: correctly name relationship types at both the first and third steps; trace consequences that change the component type across steps (e.g., from biotic to abiotic); comparative sentences name a specific structural feature shared across cascades (e.g., 'in all three, a biotic change leads to an abiotic consequence within two steps'). Weak responses: complete the table with plausible content but name relationship types incorrectly or inconsistently; comparison sentences restate the scenario descriptions rather than identifying an underlying pattern; the third-step relationship type is left blank or incorrectly classified.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the full three-row table may begin with the decomposer scenario, which is the most familiar from class work, and complete one row before attempting the others. Students with strong analytical capacity can be asked to add a fourth scenario of their own design — one that produces a cascade with both ecological and human welfare consequences — and complete its row independently.
OPEN_TASK.teacher_note_on_substitution: The teacher may substitute this task with any other format from the Science open-task menu — for example, a predict-and-explain task using a described but unfamiliar ecosystem disruption — provided the substituted task still requires the student to classify relationship types, trace a cascade of at least three steps, and compare patterns across cases.
